title: The god who thought he was permanent
hookLine: Baka the Brahma believes his heaven eternal; the Buddha shows him otherwise

lines: THE BEST PLACE IN THE WORLD.
BAKA, A BRAHMA GOD, AND HIS THEORY.
cards: Somewhere there's a person who has lived in the same town all their life and will tell you, kindly and firmly, that it's the best place in the world. They may be right.
But they've never been anywhere else, so how would they know? Now make that person a god, living in a radiant heaven so long that he's forgotten arriving.
His name is Baka, a Brahma god, and he has a theory about his home.

teach.b: This is the forty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the invitation of a Brahma. Baka holds this view: this place is permanent, eternal, complete.

Here nobody is born, ages or dies, and there's no escape beyond it, because nothing is beyond it. The Buddha, knowing the god's thought, appears in his heaven. Baka welcomes him warmly and repeats his claim.
Baka has fallen into ignorance, the Buddha says: he calls permanent what is impermanent.
Then Mara, the tempter, slips into the scene, speaking through one of the god's assembly: don't contradict the Brahma, he's the creator, the lord of all. The Buddha sees through it. I know you, Mara.
Then he shows Baka what Baka hasn't seen.

teach.h: REALMS YOU DON'T KNOW, LIVES YOU FORGOT
teach.b: There are other realms, higher and more radiant, which you don't know and can't see. And you yourself once lived in one of them, and have forgotten. Then comes a contest.
Baka says: I'll vanish from you. He can't.

teach.h: THE GOD CAN'T VANISH; THE BUDDHA CAN
teach.b: The Buddha says: I'll vanish from you. He does, and speaks a verse, his voice heard while his body can't be seen. The god and his whole assembly are astonished.
Under the drama is the point. Even a long, bright life in a heaven is still a life: arisen, and so it will pass. Baka wasn't wicked.
He was comfortable, and comfort mistook itself for forever. Look back at this week: a true samana, ten courses, Dhammadinna, four drinks, a teacher examined, daggers set down.
Each pointed past something that only looked final.

how: In Buddhist cosmology even the Brahma gods live long but finite lives; teachers use stories like Baka's to show that no state of existence, however blissful, is permanent, and reflection on impermanence (anicca) is a traditional meditation subject.

o: impermanent: it arises, and it passes
unlucky, a sign of bad fortune
eternal, the way the heavens are

games.q: who's who in Baka's heaven — tap the pairs.
p: a Brahma who thinks his home is eternal
speaks through one of the assembly
real, but Baka can't see them
Baka can't vanish; the Buddha can

s: in this story Baka is a wicked god
he isn't wicked; he's comfortable, and has mistaken a very long life for forever.
the Buddha tells Baka he once lived in a higher realm and forgot
he points to higher realms Baka doesn't know, and to the god's own forgotten past in one of them.
Mara defends the Buddha in the story
Mara speaks through the assembly, urging the Buddha not to contradict the Brahma.

games.q: you're the Buddha, in a heaven whose god insists it's eternal. a voice from the assembly warns: don't contradict him, he's the lord of all. what do you do?
o: say: I know you, Mara, and gently show the god what he hasn't seen.
games.why: the Buddha recognizes Mara behind the voice, then shows Baka realms beyond his own and the impermanence of even his long life.

practice: Find one thing it's easy to assume will always be there, your health, a parent, your job, this exact version of yourself, name it quietly, and add: for now. My health, for now. This friendship, for now.
Don't panic or argue; notice whether it feels sadder, or more precious, or both, and let it rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Anicca. Impermanent: what Baka the Brahma, so long in his bright heaven, mistook for eternal.

orig.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. Baka calls permanent what the Buddha calls anicca.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing is forever. Even a god's long, bright life arises and passes. That's a week.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 49, Brahmanimantanika Sutta (the invitation of a Brahma)
